subject: Vectorized MA(Q) model in the manual

messages.author: 146bc26797d1c5e2
messages.subject: Vectorized MA(Q) model in the manual
parts:
The MA(Q) model in the manual has two identical-looking loops, one in the transformed parameters block, one in the model block. 

I needed a shorter version to demonstrate Stan and ended up with this:

data {
  int<lower=1> N; real y[N]; 
  int<lower=1> D; // Maximum lag. 
}
parameters {
  real baseline; real trend; 
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  vector<lower=-1, upper=1>[D] theta; 
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] eta; 
  { vector[N] err;
    for (t in 1:N) { 
       eta[t] <- trend*t + baseline; 
       for (lag in 1:D) { if (t>lag)  eta[t] <- eta[t] + theta[lag] * err[t-lag]; }
       err[t] <- y[t] - eta[t]; }}
}
model { y ~ normal(eta, sigma); }

(Irrelevant to the point, the variable names are different from the manual, as are the priors, and the mu depends on t here, and this code has 'if' instead of max(). For some odd reason, variable 'T' still causes problems in my rstan.)

This seems to be about as fast as the version in the manual, and it does not duplicate code as much.

Are there some advantages to the version in the manual?

We may need to re-open the issue, but none of us
coudl reproduce it.

Which C++ compiler are you using and on which platform?
> This seems to be about as fast as the version in the manual, and it does not duplicate code as much.

The vectorization should actually make it substantially faster.

It's slightly different in that it models the t=1 and t=2 terms.

It's also slightly different in that there are no priors on
the baseline, trend, or sigma terms; in your model, theta gets a proper
uniform prior on (-1,1) from its constrained declaration.

I'll update the manual version to look more like yours
and thank you in the acknowledgments for the suggestion.
> Are there some advantages to the version in the manual?

None at all. I like yours better (modulo the missing priors).

- Bob
